Interviewer:	I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing. We’re interviewing people – women from all the different engineering disciplines. We’re focusing on placement students because we want to know about women’s first experience of the engineering industry, but we’re also interviewing non-placement students to get an idea about why they decided not to go on placement, if they’ve had any other work experience, and also about why they decided to do engineering in the first place, and things like that. So I’ll start off just asking you some background questions and then move on to ask you about your course and things like that, so … Its automotive engineering that you’re doing isn’t it?

Subject:	Yes

Interviewer:	What ‘A’ levels did you do?

Subject:	I did Maths, Further Maths, Business and Graphics.

Interviewer:	Ok, what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know. It was an all girl’s school but it was just a er – its not private, whatever that is.

Interviewer:	Was it a grammar school or just a comprehensive, but an all girls school?

Subject:	Yes

Interviewer:	Have you got any experience in the industry at all?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Are either of your parents engineers at all?

Subject:	No, my Dad works for [company] and my Mum’s a dental hygeniest.

Interviewer:	So when and why do you think you decided to do engineering?

Subject:	Well it was between – well my ‘A’ levels were either Maths, Business or Graphics, and I could do any of them really. But I messed up my Graphic design, and I didn’t want to do straight business studies, ‘cos I’d get bored I thought. And the idea of straight Maths didn’t appeal to me to much either. Cars was always just an interest I had, so it just seems like a thing where I could do a bit of everything.

Interviewer:	Do you think anything else influenced you? Did you have any careers advice?

Subject:	I went to careers advice but it was pretty much I could do whatever I wanted to do. But graphics – you had to be good at what you did to get a good salary, whereas engineering is more, you’re gonna get this starting. So that probably swayed me a little bit more, but …

Interviewer:	Were you’re family supportive of you wanting to do engineering?

Subject:	Yes, they just – well whatever I wanted to do – they’re fine with.

Interviewer:	Did you ever consider doing any of the other types of engineering?

Subject:	No I didn’t really. I didn’t want to do Mech Eng because erm. What appealed to me was the car aspect of it. So erm, thinking about it now, I maybe should have looked into aeronautical engineering because that would’ve appealed to me as well, but otherwise no.

Interviewer:	What is it then that appeals to you about automotive engineering?

Subject:	It was the – I’ve always been interested in – followed Formula 1, so it was the idea that I could maybe have some sort of career related to that. But it was just – I don’t really know, I’ve always liked cars – I think it might have been my Dad’s fault. It’s always been there, so it made sense.

Interviewer:	Ok, how did you decide to come to [this university]?

Subject:	 [University 2] was too far away because I live in [town]. I hated [university 3]. Erm, I think [this university’s] the only one that interviewed me, and they reduced the, because I didn’t have physics, I thought I’d have to do the foundation course first, but they said I didn’t have to. But actually I hated it when I came here – it was raining. But it came down to the fact that it was – it looked like one of the best courses in the country – they had all the um, well their research. I mean the selling point at [university 2] was that they had their own lecture theatre. That was literally their selling point. Then you came here and they had vibration free rooms and engine test beds and glass so you could see into the engine, wind tunnel, it was just, it wasn’t really much of a comparison.

Interviewer:	Did you realise that engineering was so male-dominated?

Subject:	Yes I did, we were warned.

Interviewer:	Did it bother you at all?

Subject:	A little bit because being at an all girls school, but erm. I don’t know, just, it wasn’t really a deciding or undeciding factor. It was just that’s what it was, so deal with it type thing.

Interviewer:	Were you encouraged to do more traditionally male subjects being at an all girls school?

Subject:	No, I think we just had a er – the sixth form was mixed, but the girls school itself it was just a broad, do whatever you wanted. I mean it might have been limited on some of the technical things but not really – we could still do all types of technology if we wanted to.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	Yes. I think some people probably have the point of view that it is just for the male dominated but, I don’t know. Most of my friends – it just didn’t really appeal to them, so I suppose its about changing the image more than the … because its no different to any other subject.

Interviewer:	Do you think that women need more information about what engineering is in the first place?

Subject:	Probably, I don’t know. My course is very much maths based, its not like you’re a mechanic or anything. But I think perhaps all that’s last – I think more information would help.

Interviewer:	What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Very organised, erm, good logical and mathematical skills. I think you’ve got to have a good sense of humour as well to get you through.

Interviewer:	Would you say that any of those characterisitics are more male or female characteristics?

Subject:	Not especially, I don’t know. I think I’m probably the most disorganised person on the course. But yes, it just depends on the individual really.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Well we’ve found that there are definitely advantages because the boys like to help you a lot, which is all good. Erm, I don’t know, you could argue maybe that from a social point of view it’s a bit different but …

Interviewer:	What do you mean from a social point of view?

Subject:	I don’t know, its just, you can’t talk about shopping all day if you want to, but you do anyway, really. But short of that, it doesn’t really make any difference.

Interviewer:	Ok, has the course been what you expected it to be so far?

Subject:	Pretty much, it’s been more theory based than design, but I think we needed to do that before we could do the design and that comes next year so, its um, yes.

Interviewer:	What about the gender proportions? How many girls are there on your course?

Subject:	Two, me and [name].

Interviewer:	Out of how many?

Subject:	There’s – I think there were 62 of us, 60 of which are boys, but I think that’s diminished slightly this year.

Interviewer:	What do you think are the best and the worst things about the course?

Subject:	Erm, I’m not sure. I know in the first year I had nearly swopped courses, mainly because I decided it wasn’t for me, but I some how managed to pass my exams, and then they were like you may as well just see how you do in the summer, and I passed them again. And this year’s been a lot more enjoyable. I think the satisfaction when you’ve got something that works, that’s really the best bits. But the worse is just, you can spend hours trying to draw a graph, that’s really not that hard, but it’s so much easier when you know what the answer is, but getting to that point, its just – drives you up the wall.

Interviewer:	Is that the type of thing that was putting you off last year then?

Subject:	I think last year I just, I wasn’t sure if I should have done graphics or not. I think it was just the change in going to uni as well. I got home at Christmas and was just like I don’t want to do this anymore. But erm, I’m glad I didn’t change I think, yes.

Interviewer:	Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	One I think, she did the vibration module and dynamics, so we had her for a couple of weeks, and we had one for business studies but that’s not really engineering.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that the female lecturers treated you the same as the male lecturers?

Subject:	Yes they did.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the male lecturers treat you the same as the male students?

Subject:	I think so. Erm, we have one lecturer that just jokes with us, but other than that, they all pretty much treat us the same way. I think, when I tried to give up they were certainly – I think even getting here because we didn’t have physics, we both found that it was, oh girls, do anything we can to get girls on the course. But otherwise its all, we don’t have a problem at all.

Interviewer:	Do you mind the jokes and stuff then?

Subject:	No, I think we deserve them.

Interviewer:	What sort of comments do you get then?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know, they’re just erm. They usually ask us a question and we don’t know the answer, so we just get laughed at, but they do that to anyone really, it just, it’s how the boys are.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’d have found it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Maybe, I’m not – I don’t think it affects me really, I just, I’m here to learn so whatever.

Interviewer:	Have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	Male.

Interviewer:	Are you happy with that personal tutor? Are they approachable? (yes) You wouldn’t rather have a female tutor?

Subject:	I think personally that I’ve had male tutors at school so it doesn’t really, no I don’t think it makes much difference.

Interviewer:	Ok that’s fine. Is there anyone or anything that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

Subject:	Erm, I think the group of friends that I have on the course, probably help me through it, but short of that nothing really.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you had to do much group work as part of the course?

Subject:	We have this year, it’s been interesting. It’s all part of the learning experience so …

Interviewer:	Do you enjoy doing group work then?

Subject:	It depends on your group and what the project is, but erm, generally I think its probably easier because you end up helping each other out. You’ve just got to make sure you’ve got a good group.

Interviewer:	Do you get put into groups then or do you get to choose who you work with?

Subject:	It’s a mixture of both, it depends. Labs you tend to be put into groups, but are two main projects, we’re actually given a choice to specify what you wanted to do and then, so I’ve ended up with people I want to be with, so its ok.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you often get to work with the other girl on your course then, or are you usually with … ?

Subject:	I don’t think we’ve ever been put in a group together actually.

Interviewer:	So you always work in groups with men? (yes) Ok, do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Yes, I think – I’d say different people bring different things. But, it depends on the personality of the person. I think may be girls seem to be more conscious about appearance. I think maybe – but then our group leader at the moment has given us a 4 page file on what our report should look like so it’s swings and roundabouts, I think maybe, yeah.

Interviewer:	Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Erm, not really no – we just had – our group at the moment, our group leader’s just a genius so he’s organised everything and its all been fairly easy. But the other project we had, it was interesting – we had one guy who has asked me out before which wasn’t a good idea, and the other guy was a safe guy and then he gave me a valentines card, so it just got a bit scary, but it was fine. But erm …

Interviewer:	What do you think are the advantages of doing group work then?

Subject:	You get different opinions and just instead of one point of view you’ve got more. But it can be a pain sometimes when you end up trying to – just confusing yourselves. But generally, you find that you end up doing something better.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the experience will benefit you when you go to work as well?

Subject:	Yes, you learn to work with other people, learnt to get by and be patient.

Interviewer:	Why did you decide not to go on a placement then?

Subject:	Well initially I was on the sandwich course and I applied to a couple of places and one I went to an interview for, which – it was a good experience, but I didn’t actually really want it because it was North Wales, and ideally I want to get a placement at home, which I just couldn’t find anything, and it got to the point where there wasn’t really anything I wanted to do and I thought I’d just be doing it for the sake of doing it. And the group of people on my course who I’m happy with aren’t doing it, so I’d lose that, so its just – makes more sense to stay here. I think what I’ll do is switch to the Masters instead, so I’ll still do 4 years. And try and get some summer placements, so I’ll get the best of both worlds.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to going on the placement?

Subject:	I’d say the experience helps a lot, just – I think half of it with me is working out if that’s what I want to do – and I’m still not sure, I might just do my Masters in Business Studies or something. But that’s the nice thing about engineering degrees – you can do that. But I think certainly from a boy’s point of view having the experience is a good thing.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you know what type of company you’d like to work for when you’ve finished?

Subject:	I think, engineering wise I don’t think – I might still do a design type thing but otherwise its probably more a business orientation thing. Then the automotive industry still appeals to me, so maybe if I could link it altogether – then I’d have the technical knowledge as well to help.

Interviewer:	When you’re applying to placements or looking for a job, what sort of things do you think will attract you to the company? Apart from the type of work that you’re doing, will it be like, location, money, training opportunities, things like that?

Subject:	I think image (lost words), pay, and location. But I just want to do something I enjoy.

Interviewer:	Is there any bits of the teaching or advice that you’ve had that you think will help you when you start work? (erm) Do you think that you will use the technical skills that you’ve learnt or do you think it’ll mainly be generic skills?

Subject:	I think it’s a bit of both. The only time you really feel like you’ve learnt something is when you do a piece of coursework, but that’s quite specific. But I think it’s the methods you apply to that that’s going to be used in industry, just how you set about doing your work. But its all fairly specific to whatever project you’re doing. But we’ve got – I think the base will be there. But its about moving on and learning whatever you’re doing.

Interviewer:	Ok, if you do go to work in the engineering industry what do you think will be the best and worse things about that?

Subject:	I think the best will be knowing that you’ve made something, so if you’re in town and see a car, you’re like, yes I designed that (lost words) and you know that you’ve done something. The worse I think will be trying to work out how to design it, I don’t think – I think that’s my problem, its not, I don’t know. Yes, I don’t think …

Interviewer:	Do you think that the course and the university experience prepares you for the workplace?

Subject:	Probably not. I don’t know, the work load I should imagine will help you with your organisation and the interaction with people will certainly help. But I think in the industry it’s going to be what 7 hours a day and we don’t do that at all really. Its just, yes I think its just aspects of maybe organisation skills.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it should be more geared to prepare you for what it’s going to be like?

Subject:	Possibly, but I’m not sure how that would work in a learning environment, I don’t know, it’s just different.

Interviewer:	Ok, what do you think you’ll be doing in 5 years time?

Subject:	Hopefully in a well paid job, I just don’t know what that is yet. Or maybe just happily married and settled. I think – we were talking about it a while ago, girls attitudes seem to – at GSCE we’re very much yes we want to be a top flyer and get paid loads, but as we’ve got older, its like well, I’m quite happy to settle and just sit at home all day. But erm, I don’t know. I think ideally, a good paid job.

Interviewer:	What do you think would be your ideal career then?

Subject:	Ideal? I want to be a presenter on Top Gear (I love Top Gear) It’s good isn’t it? Or, yes that’s what I want to do. We thought we’d make a new girly one, but erm, yeah …

Interviewer:	What is it about engineering that made you think that’s not what you’ll do career wise?

Subject:	It’s just, I think I struggle sometimes to see new concepts. I’d be able to work out how the existing one works, but to be able to design a new one, I think I just worry that I wouldn’t be able to do that, or improve a system. I think probably self-confidence, but erm, also I don’t think improving suspension interests me to be fair. Actually the design aspect more of the car is appealing, but from a technical view, it just doesn’t really get me very excited.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the confidence thing is a gender issue? 

Subject:	Possibly. I think for me it’s a very personal one, but erm. Its hard when [name] is just like me, so you’ve got nothing to compare it to. I know there are girls on aero who are more than happy to so …

Interviewer:	Is the other girl on your course considering not doing it career wise then?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	You said it is difficult with there only being two of you, but have you found that girls who are in engineering tend to either think about not going into the industry or to go on the design side rather than the more technical side? 

Subject:	I don’t know. I mean I’ve always been design, I’ve always had art and graphics, that’s always been my other option so I’ve always had that. I don’t think design appeals to Jenny at all. I think the whole concept just doesn’t appeal to her at the moment so … I don’t know.

Interviewer:	Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

Subject:	I don’t think so. I might, I don’t know. I might have done straight arts and just messed around, but ideally I want a better paid job than that, so probably not at the end of the day. No, I probably would have done something similar.

Interviewer:	Ok, what 5 words would you use to describe the automotive engineering industry?

Subject:	Sorry what was that?

Interviewer:	What 5 words would you use to describe the industry, or your experience of the industry?

Subject:	Five words? Its erm, fairly dynamic, constantly changing, the new technology for tomorrow’s going to be crazy. Erm, so yes, innovative, hard work, practical but creative, how many’s that?

Interviewer:	Probably about 10! (excellent) Would you describe it as masculine?

Subject:	Yes I think I would – but changing. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that the fact that it’s masculine is just about the numbers of men in the industry or is it the type of work that you do as well?

Subject:	The number of men in the industry. I think the type of work is open to anybody who – I think automotive’s slightly different because cars have never tended to be a female choice, but I think that’s all down to image as well, because its no different really. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that the situation will improve for women?

Subject:	Do you mean as in there’ll be more of them? (yes) Possibly, I think I don’t see why there shouldn’t be more women in engineering. But I think the automotive industry, you’ve got to overcome the whole masculine image of boys to start with, which is going to be harder.

Interviewer:	Do you think that will start to change, as obviously most women do drive now?

Subject:	I’d like to say it would, but I’m not sure.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think if you do decide to go into the industry, do you think that the fact it is so male dominated will cause you any problems at all?

Subject:	No more, I don’t think so. I think you’ve got to, you accept that that’s what it is so, you’ve just got to deal with it and move on. I don’t think there’s any problems as such. In fact I think it might even do us a favour because there’s so many, there’s always equal employment, it might even help us get a job more than someone else. Attitudes are changing its just taking a while.

Interviewer:	That’s everything then, thank you very much.

turns.text: Is that the type of thing that was putting you off last year then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think last year I just, I wasn’t sure if I should have done graphics or not. I think it was just the change in going to uni as well. I got home at Christmas and was just like I don’t want to do this anymore. But erm, I’m glad I didn’t change I think, yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: One I think, she did the vibration module and dynamics, so we had her for a couple of weeks, and we had one for business studies but that’s not really engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that the female lecturers treated you the same as the male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes they did.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the male lecturers treat you the same as the male students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. Erm, we have one lecturer that just jokes with us, but other than that, they all pretty much treat us the same way. I think, when I tried to give up they were certainly – I think even getting here because we didn’t have physics, we both found that it was, oh girls, do anything we can to get girls on the course. But otherwise its all, we don’t have a problem at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you mind the jokes and stuff then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think we deserve them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of comments do you get then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know, they’re just erm. They usually ask us a question and we don’t know the answer, so we just get laughed at, but they do that to anyone really, it just, it’s how the boys are.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’d have found it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Maybe, I’m not – I don’t think it affects me really, I just, I’m here to learn so whatever.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy with that personal tutor? Are they approachable? (yes) You wouldn’t rather have a female tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think personally that I’ve had male tutors at school so it doesn’t really, no I don’t think it makes much difference.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok that’s fine. Is there anyone or anything that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think the group of friends that I have on the course, probably help me through it, but short of that nothing really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you had to do much group work as part of the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We have this year, it’s been interesting. It’s all part of the learning experience so …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you enjoy doing group work then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It depends on your group and what the project is, but erm, generally I think its probably easier because you end up helping each other out. You’ve just got to make sure you’ve got a good group.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you get put into groups then or do you get to choose who you work with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s a mixture of both, it depends. Labs you tend to be put into groups, but are two main projects, we’re actually given a choice to specify what you wanted to do and then, so I’ve ended up with people I want to be with, so its ok.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you often get to work with the other girl on your course then, or are you usually with … ?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think we’ve ever been put in a group together actually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you always work in groups with men? (yes) Ok, do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think – I’d say different people bring different things. But, it depends on the personality of the person. I think may be girls seem to be more conscious about appearance. I think maybe – but then our group leader at the moment has given us a 4 page file on what our report should look like so it’s swings and roundabouts, I think maybe, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really no – we just had – our group at the moment, our group leader’s just a genius so he’s organised everything and its all been fairly easy. But the other project we had, it was interesting – we had one guy who has asked me out before which wasn’t a good idea, and the other guy was a safe guy and then he gave me a valentines card, so it just got a bit scary, but it was fine. But erm …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are the advantages of doing group work then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You get different opinions and just instead of one point of view you’ve got more. But it can be a pain sometimes when you end up trying to – just confusing yourselves. But generally, you find that you end up doing something better.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the experience will benefit you when you go to work as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, you learn to work with other people, learnt to get by and be patient.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why did you decide not to go on a placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well initially I was on the sandwich course and I applied to a couple of places and one I went to an interview for, which – it was a good experience, but I didn’t actually really want it because it was North Wales, and ideally I want to get a placement at home, which I just couldn’t find anything, and it got to the point where there wasn’t really anything I wanted to do and I thought I’d just be doing it for the sake of doing it. And the group of people on my course who I’m happy with aren’t doing it, so I’d lose that, so its just – makes more sense to stay here. I think what I’ll do is switch to the Masters instead, so I’ll still do 4 years. And try and get some summer placements, so I’ll get the best of both worlds.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to going on the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d say the experience helps a lot, just – I think half of it with me is working out if that’s what I want to do – and I’m still not sure, I might just do my Masters in Business Studies or something. But that’s the nice thing about engineering degrees – you can do that. But I think certainly from a boy’s point of view having the experience is a good thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you know what type of company you’d like to work for when you’ve finished?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think, engineering wise I don’t think – I might still do a design type thing but otherwise its probably more a business orientation thing. Then the automotive industry still appeals to me, so maybe if I could link it altogether – then I’d have the technical knowledge as well to help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you’re applying to placements or looking for a job, what sort of things do you think will attract you to the company? Apart from the type of work that you’re doing, will it be like, location, money, training opportunities, things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think image (lost words), pay, and location. But I just want to do something I enjoy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there any bits of the teaching or advice that you’ve had that you think will help you when you start work? (erm) Do you think that you will use the technical skills that you’ve learnt or do you think it’ll mainly be generic skills?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s a bit of both. The only time you really feel like you’ve learnt something is when you do a piece of coursework, but that’s quite specific. But I think it’s the methods you apply to that that’s going to be used in industry, just how you set about doing your work. But its all fairly specific to whatever project you’re doing. But we’ve got – I think the base will be there. But its about moving on and learning whatever you’re doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, if you do go to work in the engineering industry what do you think will be the best and worse things about that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the best will be knowing that you’ve made something, so if you’re in town and see a car, you’re like, yes I designed that (lost words) and you know that you’ve done something. The worse I think will be trying to work out how to design it, I don’t think – I think that’s my problem, its not, I don’t know. Yes, I don’t think …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the course and the university experience prepares you for the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably not. I don’t know, the work load I should imagine will help you with your organisation and the interaction with people will certainly help. But I think in the industry it’s going to be what 7 hours a day and we don’t do that at all really. Its just, yes I think its just aspects of maybe organisation skills.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it should be more geared to prepare you for what it’s going to be like?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Possibly, but I’m not sure how that would work in a learning environment, I don’t know, it’s just different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what do you think you’ll be doing in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hopefully in a well paid job, I just don’t know what that is yet. Or maybe just happily married and settled. I think – we were talking about it a while ago, girls attitudes seem to – at GSCE we’re very much yes we want to be a top flyer and get paid loads, but as we’ve got older, its like well, I’m quite happy to settle and just sit at home all day. But erm, I don’t know. I think ideally, a good paid job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think would be your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ideal? I want to be a presenter on Top Gear (I love Top Gear) It’s good isn’t it? Or, yes that’s what I want to do. We thought we’d make a new girly one, but erm, yeah …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What is it about engineering that made you think that’s not what you’ll do career wise?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s just, I think I struggle sometimes to see new concepts. I’d be able to work out how the existing one works, but to be able to design a new one, I think I just worry that I wouldn’t be able to do that, or improve a system. I think probably self-confidence, but erm, also I don’t think improving suspension interests me to be fair. Actually the design aspect more of the car is appealing, but from a technical view, it just doesn’t really get me very excited.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the confidence thing is a gender issue?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Possibly. I think for me it’s a very personal one, but erm. Its hard when [name] is just like me, so you’ve got nothing to compare it to. I know there are girls on aero who are more than happy to so …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is the other girl on your course considering not doing it career wise then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You said it is difficult with there only being two of you, but have you found that girls who are in engineering tend to either think about not going into the industry or to go on the design side rather than the more technical side?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I mean I’ve always been design, I’ve always had art and graphics, that’s always been my other option so I’ve always had that. I don’t think design appeals to Jenny at all. I think the whole concept just doesn’t appeal to her at the moment so … I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think so. I might, I don’t know. I might have done straight arts and just messed around, but ideally I want a better paid job than that, so probably not at the end of the day. No, I probably would have done something similar.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what 5 words would you use to describe the automotive engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Sorry what was that?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the industry, or your experience of the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Five words? Its erm, fairly dynamic, constantly changing, the new technology for tomorrow’s going to be crazy. Erm, so yes, innovative, hard work, practical but creative, how many’s that?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Probably about 10! (excellent) Would you describe it as masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I think I would – but changing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the fact that it’s masculine is just about the numbers of men in the industry or is it the type of work that you do as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The number of men in the industry. I think the type of work is open to anybody who – I think automotive’s slightly different because cars have never tended to be a female choice, but I think that’s all down to image as well, because its no different really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the situation will improve for women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Do you mean as in there’ll be more of them? (yes) Possibly, I think I don’t see why there shouldn’t be more women in engineering. But I think the automotive industry, you’ve got to overcome the whole masculine image of boys to start with, which is going to be harder.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that will start to change, as obviously most women do drive now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d like to say it would, but I’m not sure.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think if you do decide to go into the industry, do you think that the fact it is so male dominated will cause you any problems at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No more, I don’t think so. I think you’ve got to, you accept that that’s what it is so, you’ve just got to deal with it and move on. I don’t think there’s any problems as such. In fact I think it might even do us a favour because there’s so many, there’s always equal employment, it might even help us get a job more than someone else. Attitudes are changing its just taking a while.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s everything then, thank you very much.
